full_text: × Nov 12, 2026 9:26am PT Prime Video, RTP Take Portuguese Rights to ‘Gisberta,’ Leonel Vieira’s True-Crime Docuseries The four-part Portugal-Brazil co-production, directed by Vieira and Rodrigo Rebouças, marks Volf Entertainment’s first true-crime series By Emiliano de Pablos Plus Icon Emiliano de Pablos Latest South International Series Festival to Launch 2027 Investors Week, Linking Producers With Private Capital 6 days ago ‘Wednesday’ Director Paco Cabezas and Javier Ruiz Caldera, Helmer of ‘5 More Minutes,’ Talk Genre Filmmaking and Creative Risk 1 week ago ‘La Bola Negra’ Becomes Spain’s Third Biggest Spanish Hit Ever as Its Box Office Surges 8% Above Pre-Pandemic Average 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Gisberta' Courtesy of Volf Entertainment Prime Video and Portuguse public broadcaster RTP have acquired Portuguese rights to “ Gisberta – Life and Death of a Trans Woman,” a four-part true-crime docuseries from Leonel Vieira , the director-producer behind box office hit “O Pátio das Cantigas” and HBO Max thriller “O Grito.” The four 45-minute episodes are in post-production at Lisbon-based Volf Entertainment , which is producing with Brazil’s Ultravioleta . Prime Video has SVOD rights in Portugal; RTP holds free-to-air and AVOD rights. Related Stories UFC 333 Livestream: Here's How to Watch Volkanovski vs. Evloev Online for Free Brazilian filmmaker Rodrigo Rebouças (“Meninos ao Mar”) created the project and co-directs with Vieira, who also serves as showrunner. “Gisberta” revisits the 2006 murder of Gisberta Salce Júnior, a Brazilian transgender woman killed in Porto after being tortured by 14 minors from the Catholic-run Oficina de São José. The teenagers were acquitted of homicide, although some received lesser penalties or educational measures. The case sparked outrage in Portugal and Brazil. Drawing on archive footage, court records, Gisberta’s letters, interviews and dramatized reconstructions, the series traces her life from Brazil to Europe, the killing and its judicial aftermath. It also examines allegations of sexual abuse and mistreatment of children at the institution, which closed in 2010. Interviewees include relatives, friends, lawyers, journalists and people connected to the case. The project was presented at Conecta Fiction & Entertainment in Toledo in 2024, where it won two awards: Acorde music-licensing support and an invitation to Chile’s Sanfic Industria Series Lab and pitching sessions. “The Conecta awards gave the project a good boost: they were the springboard for us to pitch it to Amazon Prime,” Vieira told Variety . “With most of the financing secured between Amazon and the Portuguese cash rebate, we then approached the public broadcaster RTP, which also decided to come on board.” Vieira is also looking to French distributor About Premium Content (APC), involved in financing the project during development, for international sales. “APC is an excellent international distributor for this project, and we’re confident they will do a great job with it,” he said. Founded in 2022 and backed by an investment fund managed by Quadrantis Capital, Volf has built its slate around Vieira’s extensive film and television career. “Gisberta” marks the company’s first move into true crime. “Yes, it is Volf’s first true-crime series and, I believe, the first to be produced for a streaming platform in Portugal,” Vieira said. “We hope it does well, because we have another powerful story that we could also tell.” Volf’s credits also span the Spain-Portugal thriller “Favàritx,” released on Max and RTP. title: MotoGP U.S. Rights Head to ESPN in Deal With Liberty Media
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 12, 2026 9:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Maximo Quiles of Spain and CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team leads the field during the Moto3 race during the MotoGP Of Malaysia - Race at Sepang Circuit on November 1, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Photo by Mirco Lazzari gp/Getty Images ESPN is back in business with Liberty Media . The sports media juggernaut has inked a deal to broadcast MotoGP, the motorcycle racing circuit owned by Liberty, beginning in 2027. It’s a two-year deal that will cover both the U.S. and Latin America, where ESPN already had MotoGP rights. MotoGP’s most recent U.S. rights were with Fox Sports, and they had previously been with Warner Bros. Discovery and NBC Sports. ESPN say that the races will air on all of ESPN’s platforms, as well as on Disney+. Liberty Media, which is led by Derek Chang, owns both MotoGP and Formula 1, which left ESPN this year to move its U.S. rights to Apple TV. Liberty bought MotoGP in 2024 at a $4.5 billion valuation with a goal of building it into a worldwide brand as it has done with F1. The U.S. market, for obvious reasons, is a top priority, so ESPN’s reach is seen as a boost to that effort. “This agreement with ESPN marks an important milestone in MotoGP’s growth strategy across the Americas,” said Carlos Ezpeleta, deputy CEO of MotoGP. “ESPN’s position as one of the world’s leading sports broadcasters, combined with its strong connection with audiences across the United States and Latin America, makes it the ideal platform for us to continue expanding MotoGP’s reach and bring the sport closer to millions of people. This is an exciting opportunity to introduce MotoGP to new audiences while continuing to serve our passionate existing fan base through one of the most influential sports media brands in the world.” “ESPN and MotoGP have a strong relationship that dates back nearly 25 years, when we began bringing the championship to fans across Latin America,” added Freddy Rolón, head of global sports & talent office for ESPN. “This is a great example of how relationships that begin in one region of our international business can grow across ESPN’s global portfolio, creating new opportunities to connect different audiences with world-class sporting events.” THR

title: Industry Trio Launch Distinkt, AI-Powered Agency for Global Talent (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 12, 2026 9:20am PT Industry Trio Launch Distinkt, AI-Powered Agency for Global Talent (EXCLUSIVE) By Matt Donnelly Plus Icon Matt Donnelly Chief Correspondent @MattDonnelly Latest Skydance Succession: As David Ellison Sets His Team, Heads Are Rolling as Hollywood Finds Out Who’s Really in Charge 1 day ago Legendary Entertainment Hires Apollo Partner Aaron Sobel (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago A24 on Top: With Bigger Budgets, Better Box Office and Splashy IP, Is it Finally Time to Sell? 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Distinkt, a talent firm built for a large population of unrepresented creators and clients around the world, has launched out of Los Angeles and London. The agency will use AI workflows and human agents to connect actors, directors, producers, editors. photographers and digital creatives with opportunities in key markets. Distinkt is up and running with nearly 2,000 clients in 43 countries. Related Stories UFC 333 Livestream: Here's How to Watch Volkanovski vs. Evloev Online for Free The California-licensed company is founded by Robert Herman, Chris Gibbin and veteran communications executive Chris Day , who will serve as the agency’s chief spokesperson. Combined, they bring decades of experience across representation, film and commercial production and advertising. While not disclosed at launch, the new venture has been booking clients on varied projects including ad spots and scripted series and films since May. “We believe professional representation should be accessible to anyone with talent,” said CEO Herman. “We built Distinkt so that a significant part of the coordination and administration of agency work is managed by technology. That frees our agents to focus on judgment, evaluation and negotiation, and it means we can offer effective representation to far more of the world’s working creative talent.” Distinkt arrives at a moment when Hollywood’s legacy agencies are urgently trying to unlock the earnings of the creator economy, and talent face an unprecedented work slump as production continues to flee Los Angeles. The agency estimates there are more than two million actors unrepresented worldwide and more than 50 million creators who are earning some income. The global creator economy market size, currently $310 billion in 2026, is estimated to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033, according to a 2026 Grand View Research study. Distinkt will not ask clients to be represented exclusively, freeing up the user base to sign with other firms. Every Distinkt client receives four “AI teammates” on a proprietary platform to analyze work opportunities, as well as a panel of AI “specialists” in areas like legal compliance and contract analysis (trained and versed in guild standards in areas like the U.S., U.K., EU, EMEA, LATAM and Asia-Pacific markets). Human agents make all final decisions and broker deals. Distinkt is free of charge for talent clients, who can leverage the platform to browse opportunities and receive media and career analysis as agents hustle for work. Internal thinking at Distinkt is that the three-letter agencies like CAA and WME represent star talent at the height of their earning power. They’re going after untapped pools like the some 70% of SAG-AFTRA members they estimate do not have agents. “The traditional representation model has served the industry incredibly well and continues to serve many artists at the highest levels of their careers,” said Gibbin. “But the economics of that model inevitably mean that a huge amount of talent around the world remains unrepresented or underrepresented. Distinkt is designed to reach more of those people and give them a genuine advocate and a pathway into the creative economy.” Distinkt is currently privately held, but will likely seek investment in the coming months as clients surge. “We’re using technology to give agents superpowers, not to replace them,” said Herman. “Finding an opportunity is only the beginning. A great agent team has to understand what that opportunity is worth, know where there is room to push and fight for the best possible deal. We’ve built technology to help our agency do all of those things better.” ‘We Are the Shaggs,’ Documentary on the Legendary Cult Band, Coming to Theaters in 2027 Loading comments...

title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Blissfully Goes All Scrooge In Ti West’s New Horror-Flavored Take On Dickens Christmas Classic
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Blissfully Goes All Scrooge In Ti West’s New Horror-Flavored Take On Dickens Christmas Classic Robert Pattinson To Receive 40th Annual American Cinematheque Award ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Oscar Winner Takashi Yamazaki’s Vision Of Japan’s Most Iconic Monster Is Back Bigger Than Ever Battling An Even Deadlier Foe View All November 12, 2026 9:04am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Johnny Depp in Ebenezer from Paramount Pictures. Paramount Pictures There have been countless iterations on the Charles Dickens yuletide classic, “A Christmas Carol” which was first birthed to the world as a novella in 1843, but has been a favorite of Hollywood for nearly a century. Actors have warmed to the bah humbug of it all in various takes beginning with Reginald Owen in 1938’s A Christmas Carol to perhaps still the best, Alastair Sim in the 1951 version. George C. Scott and Patrick Stewart did well-regarded TV movies. Bill Murray did a contemporary comedic version with Scrooged. Albert Finney turned it all into a big screen musical in 1970. Even Kermit and Miss Piggy jumped on board with The Muppet Christmas Carol, and no less than Mr. Magoo in the evergreen (and personal favorite) Mr. Magoo’s Christmas Carol. In 2017 Christopher Plummer even took a whirl with Scrooge in the clever and wonderful biopic, The Man Who Invented Christmas which was all about Dickens writing the time honored tale. Related Stories News Daisy Ridley, Darren Criss, Travis Fimmel & Judy Greer Join Catherine Zeta-Jones In Tate Taylor's Marriage Counselor Thriller 'Cupid'; Filming Underway -- AFM News Johnny Depp & Ti West Land In A Chilly London For 'Ebenezer' Global Premiere It seems inevitable though that modern day master of all disguises, Johnny Depp would get a turn at bat, and in the latest version, Ebenezer , he has done just that. To say it is a perfect fit for Depp would be an understatement as he finds his own unique way into the role, but in a bit of a twist manages to unearth more humanity in Ebenezer Scrooge than previous versions that saved all that for the inevitable happy ending. Here, insufferable as he can be, this Scrooge allows us to have more empathy for the man as his own past is revealed as the source of his discontent. The other wrinkle with this version is brought by its director, Ti West , previously known as a horrormeister with the trilogy of X, Pearl, and MaXXXine , but it turns out he is a lifelong fan of the Dickens tale and found it ripe for more emphasis on its horror aspects built in with the infamous ghosts so crucial to the story. After all, the original title of the novella was “A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being A Ghost Story At Christmas”. Paramount’s campaign for the movie also leans into this with the ad line: “If You Think You Know His Story, Think Again”. Fear not though, we do know the story and this is still all very PG13 and not as bloodletting as the filmmaker’s past filmography. West , and his screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern, have too much reverance for what Dickens hath wrought to mess around with the bones of the tale we know all too well. Paramount’s marketing department wants us to believe this is all new but it really isn’t for the most part, just an excuse for Depp to play in the sandbox. Watch on Deadline Ebenezer, with fine period production design by Eve Stewart and darkly lit cinematography from Checco Varese, perfectly sets the tone as we meet Ebenezer Scrooge and his even more greedy business partner Jacob Marley (an ideal Ian McKellen ), just before Marley succumbs to a heart attack. It is Christmas Eve and neither owner was all too swell to loyal but beaten-down employee Bob Cratchit (an effective Rupert Grint ) who is anxious to spend time with his family including wife Clara ( Daisy Ridley ) and young son Tiny Tim (Freddie Lee Grey). There is also a visit from Christmas-loving nephew Fred (Sam Claflin) who can’t understand his uncle’s disdain for the holiday and what it really means. As Scrooge retires for the night, the fireworks begin, first with a view from down under from the late not-so-great Marley with a foreboding warning. Then we have a visit from the Ghost Of Christmas Past (a spirited Andrea Riseborough ) who takes him back (Arthur Conti is the younger Ebenezer) to his roots growing up, to his own family life, and most notably to his one and only true love Belle (Ellie Bamber) in a relationship doomed to failure as his early inclination for money over love seems to take hold. Here we see the human being, flawed but recognizable, taking his first wrong turn. Cue the Ghost Of Christmas Present (a dynamic turn from Severance Emmy winner Tramell Tillman ) who really turns on the gas to show Scrooge a miserable world, including for the Cratchit clan involving death and despair. West finds his deepest dive into the tropes of horror with this sequence, about as dark as any version of A Christmas Carol can get. And then it gets even darker with the Ghost Of Christmas Future (creature actor Robert Strange) who is so imposing he needs to say nothing, just show what will become of Ebenezer – and it is not pretty. It is no spoiler to reveal how it all works out and Depp clearly is having a blast playing it to the hilt. Fortunately the audience will walk out with their Christmas spirit (if not the spirits) intact. I am not sure the world needed yet another dance with Dickens and Scrooge. As mentioned at the top of this review there is plenty to savor from the cinema of Christmases Past that hold up quite nicely to revisit year after year after year, but I have to say it is satisfying to see Depp give it a go. After a very rough patch in his life and career, just like Ebenezer Scrooge, this gifted actor is seeing the light again. Producer is Emma Watts. title: More Than Half of Video Game Workers Laid Off Over the Past Two Years Are Still Unemployed, GDC Industry Report Finds
full_text: × Nov 12, 2026 9:00am PT More Than Half of Video Game Workers Laid Off Over the Past Two Years Are Still Unemployed, GDC Industry Report Finds By Jennifer Maas Plus Icon Jennifer Maas TV Business Writer @jmaasaronson Latest More Than Half of Video Game Workers Laid Off Over the Past Two Years Are Still Unemployed, GDC Industry Report Finds 5 minutes ago The Game Awards Adds Disney+ to Livestream Lineup 6 minutes ago ‘The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’ Remake Sells 5.2 Million Copies in First Four Days on Nintendo Switch 2 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Adobe Stock One third of video game industry workers say they have been laid off over the past 24 months, and more than half those surveyed say they haven’t found a new job since. According to the 15th State of the Game Industry Report, released Thursday by the organizers of the GDC Festival of Gaming, 62% say they have applied for 20 or more jobs, while 25% have applied for 100 or more. Additionally, 21% of those surveyed overall are unemployed, up from 13% in last year’s report, 9% of reemployed respondents have left the game industry and 4% have started their own companies or studios. Related Stories UFC 333 Livestream: Here's How to Watch Volkanovski vs. Evloev Online for Free “One in three (34%) respondents have been laid off in the last 24 months, up from 28% in the previous report and the number rises to 39% for U.S.-based respondents,” the report says. “Of the one-in-three, 68% were laid off in the past 12 months. Nearly half (49%) said their companies have conducted some form of layoffs in the past 12 months: 68% at AAA studios, 35% at older indie studios and 14% at younger indie studios.” GDC says 54% of those laid off say they are still unemployed. This year’s State of Gaming Industry Report is being released earlier than usual, as the GDC Festival of Gaming organizers say “this edition and reports going forward have been adjusted to release near year’s end, befitting the report’s reflections on the current state of the industry and a snapshot of the year.” The report is calculated based on the responses of over 2,600 game industry professionals, which GDC says is a 12% increase from the prior year. Additional key findings in this year’s report include 40% of game industry professionals reporting they use generative AI tools as part of their job, up 4% year over year and 57% of those say they use it daily. Per the report, “Usage is highest among those working in business operations & services (71%), at mobile-only studios (70%), and those working on free-to-play games (58%). Company policy tends to vary significantly by company size, with 27% of AAA workers feeling encouraged or pressured to use generative AI, compared to only 9% of indie studio workers.” Elsewhere in the report, 10% of respondents say they are developing for the next PlayStation and 8% for Xbox’s “Project Helix.” PC (83%) remains the dominant development platform, and the figures for PlayStation 5 (47%) and Xbox Series X/S (40%) are consistent with the previous survey. The full 15th State of the Game Industry Report can be found here . title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Gets a Creepily Effective Comeback Vehicle in Ti West’s Horror-Tinged Take on Dickens’ Yuletide Classic
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All November 12, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Johnny Depp (right) and Rupert Grint in 'Ebenezer.' Paramount Pictures Did the world need another cinematic adaptation of Charles Dickens’ classic A Christmas Carol ? Not really, considering the myriad versions that have appeared over the years, which play with regularity on television screens every holiday season. But Johnny Depp really needed a comeback vehicle, and he’s found an effective one in Ti West ’s horror-tinged adaptation that allows the actor to deliver the sort of quirky theatrical performance for which he became famous. While Ebenezer doesn’t break any new ground, other than possibly being the first version of the story not really suitable for young children, it fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status. Related Stories Movies Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer': First Reactions Movies AFM Hot Project: Daisy Ridley, Sosie Bacon, Simon Rex Join 'Get Rid of It' Considering that the director’s oeuvre consists of such films as The House of the Devil , Cabin Fever 2: Spring Fever , and the recent acclaimed X trilogy, it’s not surprising that this version of the Yuletide tale features a dark Gothic tone. Indeed, Ebenezer feels essentially like a horror film for most of its running time, featuring jump scares, grotesque visuals, and enough ghostly creatures to fuel a season of American Horror Story . It’s no wonder a terrified Scrooge pees himself at one point. Ebenezer The Bottom Line Gets the ghostly job done. Release date : Friday, November 13 Cast : Johnny Depp, Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman, Ian McKellen Director : Ti West Screenwriter : Nathaniel Halpern Rated PG-13, 1 hour 56 minutes Still, plenty of care has been taken for the movie, which features handsome visuals, excellent production design, and a stacked cast including Ian McKellen as Scrooge’s business partner Jacob Marley. Nathaniel Halpern’s screenplay expands upon the tale by providing more backstory than usual, with Marley still alive in the pre-credits prologue and demonstrating that he was just as irascible and nasty as Scrooge. Cut to seven years later, when Scrooge is at his most Scrooge-like, uttering enough humbugs to satisfy those Dickens fans. (Another nod to them is that the film is divided into “staves,” as was the author’s novella.) Soon enough, Scrooge is visited by the ghost of his former partner, who, besides carrying those infernal chains, looks decidedly worse for wear. Marley warns him that he’ll soon be visited by three ghosts who will … wait, why am I relating the story? You already know it. First, of course, is the Ghost of Christmas Past, played by a wispy Andrea Riseborough made up to look like a corpse that’s been left out in the sun. She brings Scrooge back to his early days, when his younger self (Arthur Conti, Carrie ) was in love with his fiancée Belle (Ellie Bamber), whom he subsequently lost due to his misplaced priorities. Then there’s the Ghost of Christmas Present, a surly figure played by Tramell Tillman ( Severance ), who physically decays as the visit wears on, eventually revealing horrific creatures trapped in his body. Finally, there’s the Ghost of Christmas Future (the appropriately named Robert Strange), an otherworldly apparition who introduces himself by having a crow fly out of his mouth. Interspersed with all the creepiness, which includes numerous rampaging ghosts behaving like zombies, are some moments of genuine emotion. Depp provides moving glimpses into Scrooge’s underlying humanity, from his missing his deceased partner to his anguish over having lost Belle to his pity for Tiny Tim (Freddie Lee-Grey), his employee Bob Cratchit’s ( Rupert Grint ) disabled son. Indeed, it’s when the film lets up on the frights and allows the story to breathe that it becomes most effective. The final redemption sequence, in which Depp gets to relax and show off his comic chops with the character’s newfound joyfulness as he visits nephew Fred ( Sam Claflin ) and his wife Clara ( Daisy Ridley ) with goose in tow, is a delight. Depp, outfitted with prosthetic make-up and facial hair, delivers a performance that no one would call subtle. In style, it most closely resembles a heavily made-up Albert Finney’s broad take on the character in the now largely forgotten 1970 musical Scrooge . But the actor’s charisma and star power eventually come through. Full credits Production: Domain Entertainment, Black Label Media, Motel Mojave, Wattsco, IN.2 Films Distributor: Paramount Pictures Cast: Johnny Depp, Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman, Ian McKellen Director: Ti West Screenwriter: Nathaniel Halpern Producer: Emma Watts Executive producers: Ti West, Adam Bohling, David Reid, Stephen Deuters, Jason Forman, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Molly Smith, Thad Luckinbill, Trent Luckinbill Director of photography: Checco Varese Production designer: Eve Stewart Editors: Ti West, David Kashevaroff Composer: Tyler Bates Costume designer: Catherine George Casting: Olivia Grant Rated PG-13, 1 hour 56 minutes THR

title: You Can’t See Everything: The Sneaky Problem With the Elizabeth Holmes Movie
full_text: Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All November 12, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Illustration by Christopher Hughes Logo text More than 100 years ago, a filmmaker directed the first documentary . Controversy has followed the form ever since. Nanook of the North , Robert Flaherty’s Inuit vérité, redefined way back in 1922 how we imagined cinema, but critics in subsequent decades charged him with staging scenes, sensationalizing events and substituting actors for real people. In the 1980s, Errol Morris disrupted the doc world with The Thin Blue Line , his reexamination of a Texas murder case from a decade earlier. So compellingly did Morris interrogate the incident that it led to an overturned conviction — but prompted a whole new inquest into why he reconstructed scenes. Two decades later, Michael Moore dropped the grenade of Fahrenheit 9/11 . The look at George W. Bush’s foreign policy sins brought Americans to the theaters by the millions but generated heat for what Moore exaggerated or left out. Related Stories Movies 'One in a Million' Filmmaker on the Ethical Dilemma He Faced and Learning to Let His Subject Find Her Own Way Movies Amanda Seyfried Feared 'You Can See Everything' Could "Destroy" Her Career, Says Her Opinion of Billy Evans "Only Got Worse" Yet something feels different with this decade’s documentary sensation, which doesn’t just play fast and loose with the truth, but plays fast and loose with the truth while making the truth the very subject of its inquiry. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s observational Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything , ostensibly about how much Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, are lying, has already solicited the kind of box office dollars more familiar to midbudget thrillers. Like its forebears, YCSE leaves itself open to questions about manipulation, starting with the fact that two camera setups followed every supposedly unselfconscious reaction, and the fact that Holmes initiated the project, possibly with crisis PR specialist Risa Heller, who helped place a soft interview in The New York Times at around the same time. But this time skepticism goes beyond fears of subject-nudging and selective editing. The entire YCSE project is built by people who specialize in presenting falsehoods as truth, each layer composed by someone whose very brand is deception, like a grift-y cinematic lasagna. Holmes spent years duping presidents into believing the reality she created, and in that light, how many of her utterances can be taken as honest? Did she really, for instance, not understand “Who’s on First?” or what Fielder was getting at by challenging her on what Theranos’ machine couldn’t do in reality? Fielder has made a profitable living fudging fiction into truth — a season finale of his HBO show The Rehearsal tragically convinced a child he was the boy’s own father — and his involvement here can’t but cast a wait-a-minute cloak over the exercise. What we’re seeing, what we’re not seeing, how details have been shaded to make everyone in it, including him, seem like something they may not have been. Nathan Fielder moniters the cameras in the season one finale of The Rehearsal. Even the person regarded as the most authentic — Amanda Seyfried, the audience surrogate into whose hands we unthinkingly place our trust — is a skilled performance magician who did not, previous screen appearances to the contrary, introduce writers to William Randolph Hearst, get raised by Jean Valjean or hold a contest to determine her real father on a Greek island. Yet somehow we assume that she and all of her fellow master-conjurers are here telling us what actually happened. I mean, it’s a documentary; why would they do otherwise? Fielder and Oppenheim made truth the subject of their documentary — “you can see everything,” the title promises us — and then proceeded to fillet it at every turn. It is a testament to their power as filmmakers that we come away smugly confident at how we have caught on to what Holmes is trying to do to Fielder while often staying oblivious to what Fielder has just done to us. As veteran journalist and commentator Matt Pearce wrote on Substack recently, ” ‘I’m just trying to be accurate,’ Fielder says toward the end of his film, lying through his fucking teeth.” That’s not to say the movie isn’t great fun, full of enjoyable surprises and, in the end, a compelling meditation on reality and gullibility. It also doesn’t mean we’re not the mark. On one level, perhaps none of this matters. Why get hung up on how much is “real” when the whole thing is such a damn good time at the theater? Yet the movie’s blunt force comes precisely from that documentary categorization; fully invent the exact same film and YCSE loses a lot of its power. But even more important than what the documentary does for Fielder is what Fielder does for, or to, the documentary; such a good time risks turning the category, currently our most important broadcast investigative medium, into one more ennui-inducing vehicle for postmodern winkiness, a perhaps not-great development in an ecosystem where shared facts are already gasping for air. In such a context, other fast-and-loose criticisms raised against docs this season — Alex Gibney’s decision to create and deploy a speaking avatar of Elon Musk using his own words in Musk , or Ava DuVernay’s deployment of AI to bring archival photos to life in The 14th — seem like peccadilloes. And yet all come as part of the same set of questions. Documentary has entered a double reckoning, both technologically in this deepfake age, given how easily something can be made to look real, and ethically, given how much harder it can be in an era of echo-chamber truth to know what “real” is in the first place. Elon Musk in Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk . Alex Brandon/AP Images Into this morass, a further irony: a movie that’s largely scripted but may paint a truer picture. Ali G has lost something off his fastball since he and the Sacha Baron Cohen who disappeared into him gleefully confronted public leaders on HBO two decades ago with his convicted stupidity, revealing what lies behind the politesse of an ATF officer, a surgeon general and Donald Trump. And yet at his best, Baron Cohen in his new movie still pulls off all the spiritual aims of the season’s big documentary, only without hiding behind that word’s protective shield. Ali G: Who Iz I? picks up on the lab experiment Baron Cohen started in 2018’s Showtime series Who Is America? Perhaps it should come as no surprise that working with and learning from him on that show nearly a decade ago was one Nathan Fielder, who came to understand both the combustive power of unmasking foolishness onscreen and how much more explosive the chemical reaction would be if you just pretended everything was real. Every era gets the brand of documentary it deserves. In a time of rampant disinformation and unabated conspiracy theories, when nobody believes anything they (or their algorithm) haven’t curated and everyone resists attempts by others to try to change their mind, when every person speaks their own “truth” and decades of relativism has turned objective facts into a hilarious fiction, YCSE is, for better or worse, our most emblematic work. The film opens a new window, all right, not on Holmes but on us, staggering among the postmodern wreckage like a marooned sailor who still hasn’t come to terms with the fact that his ship is gone. You Can See Everything is a fascinating snapshot of our social state. I’m just not sure it’s a documentary. Sacha Baron Cohen in Ali G: Who Iz I? title: Searchlight Pictures Enters Merch Partnership With Universal Music’s Bravado (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All November 12, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich in 'Wild Horse Nine.' Diego Araya Corvalán/Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures Bravado, the merchandising arm of Universal Music Group , is entering a partnership with Searchlight Pictures , the companies announced on Wednesday, marking the first time Bravado has worked with a film studio on merchandise. Bravado and Searchlight are starting the partnership with merch for Wild Horse Nine, including t-shirts as well as a bowling bag, signet rings, a scarf, passport holder and keychain among other offerings. They’re also selling vinyl from the film’s soundtrack. “We’re excited to partner with Bravado to explore new and innovative ways to bring Searchlight films to life beyond the screen,” Matthew Greenfield, President of Searchlight Pictures said in a statement. “Their creative vision and forward-thinking approach make them a great fit for our studio, and Wild Horse Nine is an exciting first opportunity to push creative boundaries together.” Bravado handles branding and merchandise for a wide swath of superstars including the Rolling Stones, the Beatles, Post Malone, Guns N’ Roses, and A$AP Rocky among many others. Bravado’s clientele is mostly music brands, though the company also works with Harley-Davidson and Travis Pastrana’s Channel 199. Searchlight represents the first time a film studio has partnered with Bravado on merch and reflects the merch company’s broader strategy in looking to court new business. The deal comes months after Bravado appointed Dan Goldberg as SVP of Strategy & New Ventures, where he was tasked with finding new verticals for the company beyond its typical music partnerships. “Searchlight has built an incredible catalog of films that people have real connections to and we’re thrilled to be working with them as our first partner in film and entertainment,” Goldberg said in a statement. “Great films create lasting fandom, and we see a real opportunity to build on that through products and experiences that extend those stories beyond the screen.” THR

title: Damian Lewis to Star in Paramount+ Soccer Comedy ‘Day 1s,’ Matthew Vaughn Directing

The streamer has greenlit a comedy called Day 1s set in the world of the English Premier League. Damian Lewis ( Billions ) will star in the series, which also counts soccer greats Cristiano Ronaldo and Thierry Henry among its executive producers. title: Dark Comedy ‘Honeyjoon’ Returning to Theaters As Launch Film for John Fithian’s New Venture
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 12, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Honeyjoon' Inés Gowland The Tribeca award-winning indie dramedy Honeyjoon by director Lilian T. Mehrel will return to theaters in early 2027 as a launch film for the Fithian Group’s theatrical marketplace platform Attend. The announcement was made Wednesday at the American Film Market , where Mehrel took part in a panel on using technology and data, including the Attend marketplace, to transform indie film distribution. Honeyjoon , a dark comedy starring Jackpot! actor Ayden Mayeri and Amira Casar and about a Kurdish-Persian mother and her American daughter vacationing in the Azores after a major loss, had an earlier limited theatrical release by Utopia’s arthouse label Circle Collective in summer 2026. Mehrel will now expand her theatrical rollout using the digital and marketing platform offered by The Fithian Group that matches producers and filmmakers directly with cinemas without having to partner with a traditional distributor. Fithian Group founding partner Patrick Corcoran in a statement said “we are thrilled to collaborate with Lilian on the theatrical expansion of Honeyjoon with Attend. She is the kind of bold visionary filmmaker that we want to launch our platform. We can’t wait for more audiences to share this unforgettable theatrical experience.” That will follow Honeyjoon winning the $1 million AT&T Untold Stories Award after premiering at Tribeca in 2025. The film went on to play around 50 festivals, including the Tribeca Lisboa Festival in Portugal a year ago, and win over 25 audience and jury awards. Now John Fithian — who founded The Fithian Group after heading up the National Association of Theatre Owners along with two of his longtime lieutenants at NATO, Corcoran and Jackie Brenneman – has tapped Honeyjoon as a curated inaugural film to launch Attend. The goal of Attend is to match a movie like Honeyjoon with the right makeup of cinemas based on various data. A filmmaker will upload various data into the platform, which will use AI to determine where best the movie might perform. Mehrel said of her distribution deal with Attend in her own statement: “The audience response led the way. Every screening, audiences burst into laughter and tears and share that the film makes them feel alive… they made it clear that Honeyjoon needs to be shared in more theaters, for more people to discover and share this special experience. I’m so excited to do that with Attend.” THR

title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Scowls His Way Through a Spookily Atmospheric but Redundant ‘Christmas Carol’ Retread
full_text: × Nov 12, 2026 9:00am PT ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Scowls His Way Through a Spookily Atmospheric but Redundant ‘Christmas Carol’ Retread Tinged with horror, as one might expect with Ti West at the helm, the umpteenth adaptation of the seasonal standard isn't a Scrooge-up, but who exactly is it for? By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest Remembering Sebastián Lelio, an Auteur Who Centered Women’s Stories With Style and Sensitivity 4 days ago ‘Jimmy’ Review: Cornball James Stewart Biopic Gets the Manner, but Not the Man 6 days ago ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Football Heroes Take to the Battlefield in Peter Berg’s Emptily Macho WWII Epic 2 weeks ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection “Before he was Scrooge he was Ebenezer ,” claims the poster for “Ebenezer,” which seems a bit of a desperate lie. The character of Ebenezer Scrooge did, presumably, have a first and last name at all stages of his life, both of them quite well-known to anyone even tangentially acquainted with Charles Dickens’ novella “A Christmas Carol” — of which Ti West ‘s handsomely produced, Gothically flavored new film is the latest in a countless string of adaptations. Other marketing materials at least acknowledge the familiarity — “The name you know, the story you don’t,” runs another tagline — while still positioning “Ebenezer” as some kind of origin story or alternative spin on an oft-told tale. Related Stories UFC 333 Livestream: Here's How to Watch Volkanovski vs. Evloev Online for Free The biggest surprise of the film, however, is that it’s really no such thing. A mostly straightforward take, albeit with slightly grislier ghost effects than most viewers will be used to, it tweaks and pads the narrative here and there — but not in ways drastic or daring enough to justify all this revisionist framing. That’s more of a relief than it is a disappointment — an edgelord “Christmas Carol” wasn’t on anybody’s holiday wishlist — but you can see why the powers that be at Paramount may have been inclined to exaggerate matters a little. As it is, the most unique selling point of “Ebenezer” is the retro Hammer horror styling that one might expect from West, the indie-rooted genre classicist behind “The House of the Devil” and the “X” trilogy. Yet this PG-13 release also stops some way short of being an outright horror film, faithfully upholding Dickens’ sentimentally redemptive arc and meaning-of-Christmas message. Too frightening for many children and too old hat for many adults, then, “Ebenezer’s” commercial prospects thus rest on its biggest gamble: the casting of Johnny Depp in the title role. Back from the international arthouse wilderness after eight years on the A-list blacklist, Depp returns to studio cinema to take on the kind of flamboyantly transformative, pantomime-style part that he used to do on the regular for the likes of Tim Burton and Gore Verbinski. Slathered in peaky old-age prosthetics, with a hunched, craggly demeanor and short, snarly vocal inflections, he makes for a perfectly solid, by-the-book Scrooge — with occasional moments of ripe inspiration in his line readings — without ever broaching the pained, soulful depths of, say, Alastair Sim’s gold-standard screen incarnation from 1951. It’s perhaps canny that Depp has chosen for his comeback vehicle a character who hardly demands to be loved: How much viewers are individually rooting for the star himself may determine how much they share in the film’s warm-and-fuzzy payoff. For the most part, however, “Ebenezer” is a pretty chilly affair, beginning with a needless prologue that details just how Scrooge’s cantankerous business partner Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen) became Marley’s ghost one frosty Christmas Eve; jumping ahead seven years to a mood of near-identical misery in Scrooge’s loan office, as he grudgingly grants his put-upon clerk Bob Cratchit (Rupert Grint) the next day off, lends proceedings an additional layer of déjà vu. From there we check off all the well-worn story points, as Scrooge spurns the seasonal requests of charity collectors and his earnest nephew Fred (Sam Claflin) alike, before taking to his bed so Marley can cue the phantom parade. Even if you’re shrugging through this with a been-there-done-that air, you may still be startled by the sheer freakiness of Andrea Riseborough’s appearance as the Ghost of Christmas Past: a wheezy, tulle-swaddled ghost bride with boiled-egg eyes and an eerie one-syllable-at-a-time manner of speech. She’s sufficiently unnerving, in fact, to distract us from some light embellishment of the relationship between the young Ebenezer (Arthur Conti) and former fiancée Belle (Ellie Bamber) — which, along with a supposedly upbeat but bleakly capitalistic change in Cratchit’s professional standing, represents the greatest liberty taken by Nathaniel Halpern’s generally rote script. Tramell Tillman brings some compellingly surly energy to his Ghost of Christmas Present, here an ailing, antagonistic type with spirit-skin cracking like scorched earth; Daisy Ridley draws the shortest star-casting straw as Fred’s modern-minded wife Clara. It all ticks along efficiently enough, never exactly dragging — not least because you generally know exactly what’s coming next — but never stirring the heart in the way the best “Christmas Carols” do. For viewers not invested in the Deppaissance, the rewards of “Ebenezer” are chiefly ones of atmosphere and craft — things that West, attentive to detail from the luridly scarlet, 1960s-style opening credits onwards, doesn’t skimp on. Production designer Eve Stewart is the film’s clear MVP, going heavy on the blackened timber and mildew in her dank, crooked re-creation of Dickensian London, well served by Checco Varese’s charred, coaly lensing; you can practically smell the sour rot here, everywhere from sidewalks to soft furnishings. Even when the film gives in to Yuletide cheer, it retains a frost-bitten edge, both visually and spiritually: This is one “Christmas Carol” where you sense, by the end, that the reformed Scrooge may just have held onto a cold, hard nugget of cruelty. A change of heart is for life, after all, not just for Christmas. ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Scowls His Way Through a Spookily Atmospheric but Redundant ‘Christmas Carol’ Retread Reviewed at Charlotte Street Hotel screening room, London, Nov. 9, 2026. title: Patrick Hoerl’s Autentic Buys Gedeon Media Group’s Assets & Launches Studio
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Jeff Goldblum To Narrate Cliburn Piano Competition Doc Series ‘Exit Stage Right’ ‘Line Of Duty’: Arnott, Fleming & Hastings Return To Service In First Look At Season 7 Of BBC’s Record-Setting Cop Drama Gang Dong-won & Kim Go-eun To Lead Netflix Korea Romance-Action Period Drama ‘The Twilight Between Us’ From Kim Won-suk View All November 12, 2026 8:59am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Patrick Hoerl Autentic Patrick Hoerl’s German factual specialist Autentic has acquired the assets of Gedeon Media Group (GMG), and is launching a studios business off the back of the deal. GMG was forced into judicial liquidation earlier this year by a French Commercial Court after running into financial difficulties, with Autentic among those expressing interests in a rescue deal. Autentic has now won out. The Munich-based has now established Gedeon Studios as a French production and distribution subsidiary, with GMG’s 3,000-hour catalog being subsumed into Autentic Distribution and a digital channels division going into Autentic’s channel management unit. Related Stories Executives Tubi CEO Anjali Sud, Roku Media President Charlie Collier Leaving The Fold As Fox Sets Exec Team After Roku Close News Good News Network Sold To Group Including Whalar Co-Founder James Street The asset deal includes Gedeon Programmes, Docland Yard and MC4. Gedeon filed was placed in liquidation in August, with the program units allowed to continue trading while a buyer was sought and sales arm Terranoa shuttered immediately. Watch on Deadline Gedeon Studios will oversee all ongoing GMG productions and project development, including approximately 25 hours of television programming currently in production and two feature-length documentaries. A seven-member team from the existing organization will join the new business. This includes senior producers Laurence Favreau, Valérie Guerin and Coraline Roch and Head of Development Mina Cuche. Carine Nonnenmacher, one of GMG’s senior producers, will lead the new studio, with GMG’s founder and former President, Stéphane Millière, working closely with the new company as Senior Consultant, Programme Development. Gedeon was founded back in 1996 with the creation of Gedeon Programmes, and went on to become one of France’s most well-known factual production companies and the winner of more than 500 international awards for its docs in genres such as science, archaeology, history, culture and heritage. The likes of the BBC, CCTV, National Geographic, PBS, NHK, RADIO Canada, RAI, RTS, RTVE, SBS, SVT and ZDF have all counted themselves as buyers. Autentic has a similar reputation in Germany, well established in factual genre. “With Gedeon Studios in Paris and Autentic in Munich, we will have teams in the two biggest markets in Europe,” said Patrick Hoerl, Managing Director at Autentic. “By combining the expertise of both companies, and using significant synergies in the monetization of content, will make us more resilient in the current, challenging market environment. “Over more than three decades, Stéphane Millière and the Gedeon team have built an extraordinary legacy, establishing the company as one of the most respected names in factual production. We are proud to continue that journey together with the team in France, preserving valuable expertise and creative excellence while laying the foundation for the next phase of growth.” Millière added he was “very pleased that Autentic is taking over the assets of the Gedeon Group through a new company that will continue to build on the work of the outstanding editorial team that has worked alongside me to develop the brand, carry forward ongoing projects and distribute the catalogue established over the past 30 years.” “This alliance between two strong brands and two talented teams further strengthens the potential of Autentic for the years to come. I have the greatest respect for Patrick Hoerl, who has always been a passionate advocate for the documentary genre.
